content: The systematic review included experimental and quasi-experimental studies published in English with full-text availability. These studies involved at least one physical exercise targeting upper limb strength. Two independent evaluators extracted data from each article, including study characteristics (publication year, country of origin, and study design), participant demographics (gender and age), and disability details (lesion level and cause). Evidence Synthesis: Seven articles were included in the systematic review. The studies frequently examined variables such as shoulder pain, cardiorespiratory capacity, and functionality. Results demonstrated improvements in all these variables due to training. Conclusions: Training programs improved upper limb strength, functionality, and reduced shoulder pain in individuals with paraplegia. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Maiano et al. (2019) investigated the effects of exercise interventions on balance in children and adolescents with intellectual disabilities. The review included studies published in English that used experimental or quasi-experimental designs and focused on balance improvement. Studies targeting specific subpopulations or physical characteristics were excluded. Risk of bias was assessed for randomization, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete data, selective reporting, and other biases. Results: The search identified 937 articles, with 15 studies (published between 1991 and 2017) meeting inclusion criteria. Exercise interventions were more effective than control conditions in improving static balance in children with Down syndrome and combined static-dynamic balance in children and adolescents with Down syndrome. However, findings on dynamic balance in children and static balance in adolescents were inconclusive. Interpretation: Exercise interventions appear effective in improving static and dynamic balance in young individuals with intellectual disabilities. However, the findings are preliminary due to the small number of studies and their limitations. A meta-analysis by Alphonsus et al. (2019) examined the effects of exercise, yoga, and physiotherapy on physical, mental, and social quality of life (QoL) in individuals with multiple sclerosis (MS). The review included studies published between 1990 and 2017. Standard mean difference scores were calculated for physical, mental, and social functioning domains. Results: Eighteen studies met inclusion criteria. Aerobic exercise and physiotherapy significantly improved physical, mental, and social QoL. However, yoga and combined exercise interventions did not show significant effects on any QoL domains. Conclusion: Aerobic exercise and physiotherapy improve physical, mental, and social functioning in MS patients and should be considered as part of standard treatment. A systematic review by Campbell et al. (2019) investigated the efficacy and safety of high-intensity interval training (HIIT) in individuals with MS. The review included studies published in English that used HIIT and included MS participants. Quality was assessed using the PEDro scale. Results: Seven studies (described in 11 articles) were included, with participants predominantly having mild disability. Adverse events were generally mild, with one study reporting six events, four of which were attributed to the intervention. Conclusion: HIIT appears safe and effective in improving fitness in individuals with MS and low disability levels. Further research is needed to explore its effectiveness in progressive MS and higher disability levels. A systematic review by Charron et al. (2016) examined the relationship between physical activity and physical ability outcomes in MS. The review included studies published between 2011 and 2016 that evaluated exercise interventions on physical disability outcomes in MS. Results: Twelve studies were included, examining endurance training, resistance training, and unconventional exercises (e.g., tai chi, kickboxing, vestibular rehabilitation). Endurance training improved walking ability, while mindfulness exercises and dynamic workouts improved balance and coordination. Resistance training improved lower limb strength and endurance but not walking ability. Combined resistance and endurance training improved mobility, balance, and coordination. Conclusion: Physical activity is associated with measurable benefits in physical ability outcomes, but continuation is likely required to maintain these benefits. Adverse events were generally mild. A meta-analysis by Manca et al. (2017) evaluated the effects of strength training on muscle strength and functional capacity in individuals with MS. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing strength training to no intervention. Results: Eleven RCTs (426 participants) were included. Strength training consistently improved muscle strength, with significant improvements in walking performance. However, methodological inconsistencies and inadequate reporting limited comprehensive conclusions about the impact on patient functioning. Conclusion: Strength training leads to consistent strength gains in MS patients. Methodological improvements are needed for future trials to better assess its impact on functional outcomes. An integrative review by Morrison et al. (2016) examined the relationship between physical activity and cognitive performance in MS. The review included studies addressing both physical activity and cognitive function in MS. Results: Nineteen studies were analyzed. Nine studies reported significant relationships between higher physical activity or cardiorespiratory fitness and cognitive function. Ten intervention studies showed mixed results regarding the effectiveness of physical activity in improving cognitive domains. Conclusion: While correlational studies suggest a link between physical activity and cognitive function in MS, intervention studies provide equivocal evidence. Confounding factors may have influenced results, and further research is needed. A meta-analysis by Veneri et al. (2018) assessed the effects of yoga on body structures, physical capacity, and quality of life in adults with stroke, MS, and children with cerebral palsy (CP). Results: Yoga studies showed negligible to medium effect sizes for stroke, and negligible to large effect sizes for MS and children. Yoga was comparable to other exercise modalities in improving physical progress and quality of life. Conclusion: Yoga is neither superior nor inferior to other exercise interventions for adults with stroke or MS and children. More research is needed, particularly in children and adults with CP, to develop effective yoga programs. A systematic review by Cugusi et al. (2017) evaluated the effects of Nordic walking (NW) on motor and non-motor symptoms, functional performance, and QoL in Parkinson’s disease (PD). Results: Six RCTs (221 participants) were included. NW was feasible and likely effective in improving functional and clinical outcomes in PD. However, comparisons with other exercise interventions yielded controversial findings. Conclusion: High heterogeneity and methodological discrepancies among studies prevent firm conclusions about NW’s effectiveness compared to other interventions. Further research with standardized designs is needed. A systematic review by Ćwiękała-Lewis et al. (2017) evaluated the effects of tai chi on physical function and well-being in PD. Results: Eleven studies (548 participants) were included. Tai chi improved balance and aspects of well-being, though results were mixed. Further research with rigorous designs, larger sample sizes, and adequate tai chi doses is needed. Conclusion: Tai chi shows potential benefits for physical function and well-being in PD, but more robust evidence is required before widespread recommendations can be made. A systematic review by Dos Santos Delabary et al. (2018) analyzed the effects of dance on functional mobility, motor symptoms, and QoL in PD. Results: Dance interventions improved functional mobility and motor symptoms compared to other interventions or no intervention. However, methodological limitations and small sample sizes were noted. Conclusion: Dance may benefit functional mobility and motor symptoms in PD, but further research with rigorous designs is needed to confirm these findings.
